@Eric Wieser @Johan Commelin I was thinking about exactly the junk value issue in a different context (after a talk by @Sidharth Hariharan, where he mentioned an actual error due to a junk value, and some other discussion).

I notice that over time with proof automation having become stronger, we can write a[i] for lookup in a list and it is generally automatically proved that i is legal. If not automatic, it can be added to the context. I was wondering if in principle it is better to not have junk values for a/b but require a proof that b is non-zero with automation from the context?

I realize that Mathlib was built before grind and any refactoring will be a massive effort. So my question is more about principles.

I've also been thinking about junk values and semantic alignment. Maybe we should start a new thread.
One possibility might be to have a parallel hierarchy of definitions that don't use junk values, and glue that connects X-with-junk to X-no-junk under the appropriate assumptions. Once that hierarchy is in place, it could be almost automatic to (i) generate a junk-free version of a statement that uses junk values, and (ii) a proof that the two statements are equivalent under appropriate conditions (namely conditions that ensure junk values don't occur).

Good to hear this. In a workshop last week, there was discussion on both kernel bugs and junk values. The latter came up in the context of the error during the sphere-packing theorem proof. The issue was raised that we have to check Mathlib definitions all the way down.

My response then was that since these definitions have been used heavily, errors would most likely have been found. But I realised that this was not correct with junk values - the errors are not merely found but there by construction. We hope that these will not leak out. Not very reassuring for a formal proof system.

If a junk-free option can be built (along with lean4lean proved) then we can raise our confidence in Lean proofs.
@Johan Commelin should this discussion (assuming it gets traction) move to another channel like Lean4/general? It is not only about AI?
@Siddhartha Gadgil Yes, sorry, forgot to change channel. Done now.

Siddhartha Gadgil said:

The issue was raised that we have to check Mathlib definitions all the way down.

I think this can actually be circumvented in some cases, by writing down a suitable characterization. For example, if you wanted to convince someone that MeasureTheory.lintegral is truly the Lebesgue integral and not anything else, I can think of two ways:

  1. Carefully examine the definitions all the way down.
  2. Come up with a set of properties which uniquely characterize the Lebesgue integral (e.g. linearity, dominated convergence, agreement with simple functions), and prove that lintegral is the unique object which satisfies the desired properties.

Option 2 can provide a nice alternative for sufficiently complex definitions. This is not a very original idea, and is directly inspired by the way the Jacobian challenge was set up. But I think there could be some value in 'packaging' a nice, minimal characterization for certain mathlib definitions.

Can we use the new (m)vcgen style spec syntax Lean now provides of ensures on some of our definitions? I don't think we use it at all in Mathlib currently. Would "spec" like annotation with all its keywords help here?
Do we have a list of junk value somewhere?

The point is that there are many Lean novices who are beginning to use Lean. The person raising the question said that he thought one can simply trust Lean. When I pointed out one has to check definitions he commented "definitions all the way down"

This was correct. We should be able to say that if you go to basic ones you can trust them because they have been checked and used heavily. But with junk values it is not even true that the definitions are correct.

Yakov Pechersky said:

Can we use the new (m)vcgen style spec syntax Lean now provides of ensures on some of our definitions? I don't think we use it at all in Mathlib currently. Would "spec" like annotation with all its keywords help here?

As I said above, with indices for lists we already have a method that works in standard Lean. And with grind works without too much friction.

I see the two as complementary. The List.get example is using lean machinery to exclude illegal inputs. I brought up spec and ensures, so that when you're reading a definition, you don't have to look for a separate spec lemma describing the behavior, it is tied directly into the definition.
I guess I don't understand spec well enough.

Joris van Winden said:

I think this can actually be circumvented in some cases, by writing down a suitable characterization.

We discussed that idea when Joris visited me last month and I built a small package that provides a characterization attribute (in the LeanSpec package at https://github.com/LeanMachineLearning/exposition). You put it on a property, on a theorem stating that a def satisfies it and on a uniqueness theorem (that could use any relation for the "uniqueness", for example a.e. equality).

My Referee website detects that attribute and does two things: it shows the characterization in a special section, and it uses it to show two distinct dependency graph (one for the construction, and another one for the characterization). Example at https://remydegenne.github.io/alpha-rar/referee/chapter-mathlib/module-mathlib-quadraticvariation/decl-AlphaRAR___predQuadVar/#decl-AlphaRAR_x2e_predQuadVar (you can switch the graph type at the top of the graph panel). It's not a great example because the characterization graph is larger than the trivial construction graph (and I don't have good examples for now). I expect that for the stochastic integral that we are building in the brownian motion repository the construction will use 100 new definitions but the characterization will use almost none.

I was working on documenting junk values earlier in the summer, and then tried to build a linter to detect/warn for them. Here's a repo that has the dataset of junk values I made as well as the linter (dataset in data/linter_dataset.jsonl). In the same GitHub organization, I'll also release the repo that has the code I used to generate the dataset. I hadn't worked on this in a while but if people think it would be useful I could keep developing it. Neither the linter nor the dataset are complete but any feedback would be appreciated (for example junk values missing from the dataset).

One design decision I made was to only include "junk value producing" declarations (eg def, abbrev, instance, inductive) and not any theorem/lemma declarations that prove things involving junk values. The dataset contains declarations from both Lean core and Mathlib.

It was roughly built by scraping for certain flags that indicate potential junk value presence (eg dite, Classical.choice, by_cases and docstring flags like 'junk', 'dummy', etc.) as well as Zulip for mentions of junk values. Then I had an agent judge each declaration for if it was a junk value or not and record some extra info about it (eg what's the actual junk output, what hypothesis you need to avoid the junk value, etc.). I then did a dependency sweep where I looked at all declarations that depended on the declarations I had already determined were junk, and had an agent classify these as well.

Happy to answer any questions about it!

I’m still learning Lean so this may have an obvious answer I don’t know yet: is there a reason junk values aren’t labeled as such like default values are with a Junk class or something? Even just an abbrev of Inhabited to make it clear to the human reading would help.
how would you do such a labelling?

One reasonable option seems to be an environment extension and an attribute to note the condition needed to ensure the junk value is not used. This can serve as a warning at least, next as a contract and finally to generate junk-free code.

Siddhartha Gadgil said:

One reasonable option seems to be an environment extension and an attribute to note the condition needed to ensure the junk value is not used. This can serve as a warning at least, next as a contract and finally to generate junk-free code.

The linter I sent already does this in a way. It only warns when the condition that guards against the junk value isn't present. It's kind of hard to implement fully though since sometimes it's not easy to verify if the condition needed to block the junk value is actually present. For example if you have 1/x in some theorem statement and x is a complicated expression, its hard to automatically unravel that x \neq 0 without explicitly providing this as a hypothesis. Currently it uses some simple tactics to try to automatically do this (positivity for example)

Alex Meiburg said:

Snir Broshi said:

Zixiao Jolene Wang said:

Do we have a list of junk value somewhere?

#26330

I would definitely welcome help and input with this. I think such a file should exist, hosted somewhere within the Mathlib repository, primarily for educational purposes. Possibly an extension would be showing, for each usage of a definition, how to use it with appropriate hypothesis 'guards', as well an example where a guard isn't needed. And, possibly, separately, there should be a separate file that aims to be comprehensive as documentation and testing.

I don't think that "fully comprehensive" makes sense really, because so many defs build on each other in ways that inherit junk values, it's not really clear what would constitute a "separate" junk value.

If we know the origins of the junk values, then it is easy to trace if something uses one of the originating functions. It will be more complicated to know if the function call generates a junk value though.

Note that one option sort of orthogonal to the ideas here which I've experimented with is using opaque junk values which are unique to the function they're used in as well as to each argument(s) for which that function is undefined.

Recall that an opaque value is just an element of the type that is allowed to exist because the type is inhabited, but is "equationally trivial" in the type theory. So, kind of like a "top-level free variable". Since this opaque value would be parameterized by the decl name and arguments, each undefined value is therefore different, which makes it much harder to prove "accidental" statements, while still giving you a total function. It's still not perfect, since the undefined value still is "something", just not the same thing as anything else. (Note: you get nice pretty-printing, too: e.g. undefinedValue[a / 0].)

However, while I think this would help avoid misformalization, and it definitely helps the types be more convenient (you get to still use Real instead of a subtype of Real excluding 0, or such), it does still implicitly embed a proof obligation in your definition that must be discharged when proving things about it initially. If we want junk values not just for total functions and clean types but also for "accidentally nice lemmas", like 0 / x = 0 for all unqualified x, then this is not the right approach :)

As such I'm not sure if this would be too much of a burden in practice or not; hopefully, a couple initial lemmas become more complicated than they are today, but then the "proper" API is fine and reasonable.

I consider this is complementary because it helps bulletproof against misformalization without demanding type differences or hypotheses, but still does not provide the dictionary between these sorts of junk-producing definitions and the hypothesis-taking definitions being discussed here.

Though happily it does provide a way to determine whether something intrinsically is capable of producing a junk value through metaprogramming (assuming it follows this convention), which could be useful. :)

Yes, I could upstream that characterization attribute. One issue is that it is LLM-written and I don't understand tactic writing enough to be able to vouch for the PR content or answer reviews. But it's a very simple attribute so it could be fine.

About the Referee website: trusting Mathlib is not hard-coded (you can pass --trust packageName for any package and it will exclude packageName and its ancestors from the graph) so the website could be generated for Mathlib. An issue will probably be that it would be very large so I would not be able to host it on github pages and will not be able to easily show the result here. I did not think about generating it only for some part of a repository (and not for the whole thing) but it might be easy to do. I'll try that soon.

FWIW in the Annals challenge we were very careful when applying functions which we knew could give junk answers, and at one point when formalising a statement about the least real number with a certain property we convinced ourselves that the set we were taking the inf of really was not bounded below! We contacted the author who explained that the theorem in the Annals was trivially wrong as stated and that they meant the greatest real number with that property. "That's embarrassing", they said. My point is that it's not just machines that need to be careful about junk values.

Good story to remind everyone to be cautious

I have a vision for annotating junk value. For functions and operations that can create junk value (for example, a / b), we create a second version that attaches a proof of no junk (e.g. a /'( ... : b ≠ 0) b) (The creation of such second version can be done with some metaprogramming). This junk-annotated version will not be used in any proof or internal statement, but will be used at trust boundary (e.g. the comparator Challenge.lean file). At the same time, tools like comparator can enforce that only junk-annotated expression can be used in the challenge statement.

For example, I can write Riemann hypothesis as 

theorem riemannHypothesis
(s : ℂ) (hs1: s ≠ 1)
(h1 : riemannZeta'(hs1) s = 0)
(h2 : ¬∃ (n : ℕ), s = -2 * (↑n + 1)) :
    s.re = 1 / 2 := sorry
I wonder how hard it would be to do what @aerh has suggested, i.e. doing essentially the same as docs#optParam ? Are there any obvious issues with it that I don't see?

FWIW my reflections as a blog post: https://siddhartha-gadgil.github.io/automating-mathematics/posts/lean-kernel-bugs-and-junk-values/
@Siddhartha Gadgil Your text is beautifully written and a wonderful read. Any chance you propose it to the official blog?

Very nice writing - I also think this would make a nice blog post. A few minor additions or corrections:

  • I once heard the number "8000 lines of code" for the Lean kernel (I believe in one of Leo's talks), so your "a few thousand lines (I believe)" is correct. I don't know the current number; it's probably similar.
  • "Till the beginning of August 2026, Lean had managed to maintain the record of no known kernel bugs." sounds very nice. It's not quite true, though: here is a list of Lean soundness bugs (and a few related ones). It's three weeks outdated by now, I still want to make a few tweaks to it, etc. --- but the takeaway is that soundness bugs definitely existed before, just very few. As far as I know, this list is complete to the date mentioned there.
  • I would disagree with the phrasing of "this [definitions are correct] is manifestly not the case - with junk values they are sometimes wrong". I would phrase it as "statements can be wrong, if their meaning is unintentionally different because it relies on junk values of definitions". (Standard example: example : 2 - 3 = 0 := by omega is true because this uses Nat substraction, which saturates.) To me, this difference is important --- the definition of natural number subtraction is not wrong (in the sense that you "only need to fix the definition") - but the statement is wrong because it presumably doesn't say what we want it to.

@Filippo A. E. Nuccio Thanks. I would be happy to propose this once I have made the fixes as pointed out by @Michael Rothgang

Most importantly, as far as I know the Collatz proof was the first case of a wrong proof passing the comparator, at least since Lean 4 was mature (say once the comparator was stable) - though they were cases that passed the Lean Repl for example. So I assume some corrected form of my claim holds. Is it the first case where there was a bug at the same place in all kernels? Or were the other bugs found internally and fixed, so this was the first case of a wrong proof of an important result being publicised?

As for the other point, while I will clarify my wordings, I deliberately used the word wrong for what is more precisely a semantic mismatch, given that my goal was to address non-expert Lean users. Im mathematics when something should be undefined but is defined and takes an arbitrary value, then it is regarded as wrong. Even ordinary programming languages will generally throw errors. Practically, as @Eric Wieser points out with the Anthropic proof, it puts a burden on the user to check that junk values were not used in definitions.

Even though I was always somewhat uncomfortable with junk values (especially as I really liked the feature of Lean, and Agda that I had used before, of elminating the need), I would say trusting in Lean meant check your definitions and your statements relative to what is already in the library - which should be correct because of other use and review. But hearing of the mistake made by those more skilled by far than me at Lean (leave alone my typical audience) I won't say this so long as there are junk values.

The natural number subtraction is of course the most eggregious case of semantic mismatch, something I demonstrate. But if there were only a handful of such things one could trip over, then a user could be warned (and an AI linter could easily check for abuse).
I also agree with your choice of wording. @Michael Rothgang 's proposal is certainly techincally correct, but I like your way of communicating the message to non-experts.
